item.title: My Buddy Mike, Efficiency Gains From AI, and The World’s Most Boringly Benign Criminal Conspiracy
item.description:
Note: details have been obfuscated and changed to protect – not the innocent, who are invariably vindicated by the end of act three – but the guilty, for whom the narrative provides no such guarantees.

My buddy Mike is one of a very small number of people in my life I would unhesitatingly describe as having a real job[1]. He wakes up, takes the train into work, and directly helps specific people accomplish worthwhile things. Every shift, he leaves the world a little brighter than it was when he clocked in. And for this, the Economy awards him slightly less than double the local minimum wage.

(Meanwhile, I spend about the same amount of time moving some numbers around, and am awarded approximately triple what he makes. They’re good numbers, and I move them with uncommon skill and deftness; still, it’s hard to look at the two of us and not feel like Graeber was onto something.)

Among his many mundane duties is collecting, collating and reformatting The Information. The Information is freely available on The Website, but not in the format his bosses find most palatable. So every month, when The Information is updated, he spends a full day copying it line-by-line into The Spreadsheet.

Or, rather, he spent a full day. When he told me about this, I immediately informed him that was ridiculous, and that I – with help from a then-current Frontier Model – could very easily construct a HTML/JS file he could paste The Website’s source code into, and get The Information back out in perfectly Spreadsheet-friendly format with a click of a button. An hour after I brought this up, we had a functioning proof-of-concept; two hours after that, we had a full solution.

And here our troubles began.

Mike: My employer won't let me use it yet

Me: ?!

Mike: Infosec paranoia

Mike: As I suspected

Me: What information is even being secured?! It's publicly available information!

Mike: I have a way forward tho

Me: I'd caution you against using explosives but in this case I think it's warranted

Mike: I basically just need to talk to [REDACTED]'s colleagues / boss instead of my IT department

Mike: I actually got a light telling off from my boss for not telling him about this before we started working on it.

Me: It's <200 lines of [VARIOUS OBSCENITIES] cookie-cutter HTML/js! The IT team can just, like, look at it!

Mike: See, the trouble with that is that I'm not allowed to download / send it to my work laptop

Me: Are you allowed to take your nonwork laptop to work?

Me: Or are they worried you'll use it plus your l33t hacker skillz to download all their RAM?

Mike: I'm not allowed to do work on my personal laptop, but I can probably get away with bringing it and showing them the code we already set up

Me: Would it help if I actually hosted these websites on a website?

Me: So they can just navigate to it in browser?

Mike: I asked my boss about that and he didn't like it

Me: . . .

Me: Did you get a chance to demo [THE SOLUTION] yet?

Mike: No . . . they need to get approval from [REDACTED][2] first, and I've received no updates . . .

Mike: See, this is why I need to learn HTML. Then I could persuade my workplace to let me write it on my work computer.

Me: Have you considered having your regular monitor open and just painstakingly copying every line onto your work computer by hand?

Mike: Tempted. But I'm sure I would need permission to do that, too

Me: (I'm joking, but the joke is that I don't understand what they think the problem even is.)

Mike: I don't think they understand what the problem is either, as none of the people I've actually talked to are tech savvy at all

Mike: But they're who I need to go through before I get to actually talk to an IT person

Me: "Do you have a license for that? And do you have a license-showing license?"

Mike: One of the few things I dislike about my job is that in terms of the social hierarchy, I am essentially a legume.

Mike: People are nice about it thankfully, but it does mean that I don't have power to do stuff that doesn't normally get done

Mike: Without asking permission first

Me: Can't you just call the IT dept? Or show up there?

Mike: I would have to ask [REDACTED] first

Mike: And it would have to be a day where we're not too busy, and we're actually in the same building

Me: . . . you know, I actually really like insane bureaucracies, under the right conditions.

Me: When the arbitrary constraints are just unconstraining enough that you end up with a fascinatingly-novel problem . . . and you're given enough time & leeway to fix it . . . that's pretty fun.

Me: Doesn't seem like either of us are in those circumstances atm tho.

Mike: No lmao

Mike: [REDACTED] just told me that we probably can't go through with automating this process as the website will probably not give permission for the process to be automated and will probably charge for access to the source code

Mike: So this was all for nothing

Mike: But that's wrong, isn't it? We already have the source code!

Mike: And it's a public website?

Mike: WHY IS EVERYONE SO ADVERSE TO MAKING IT EASIER TO DO A VERY BORING PART OF MY JOB

Me: That sucks.

Me: I'm not sure why you need the site's permission, they expose the info you use to the world every time someone clicks Inspect Element, or hell every time you access the site at all.

Me: At a guess I think they might be worried about you Scraping them, like, telling a robot to repeatedly automatically access their site?

Me: And they think that might chew up their bandwidth?

Me: But if anything this means you'd have to put LESS load on their servers . . .

Me: Lowkey I think the problem might have been that you asked permission.

Mike: I KNOW

Me: If you’d just gone ahead and done it no-one would care.

Me: And if you’d presented it as a fait accompli, bureaucratic logic would have grandfathered you in.

Mike: The thing is I wanted everybody else who does a task like this to ALSO be able to do it the Right Way

Mike: Can’t make that happen quietly

Me: fwiw I think this should be the heart of your argument: "We're not Scraping you so you won't end up DDOS'd, and also it's not automatic because I still have to press the big button each time (& then look at the output to make sure it's actually right)."

Mike: You're a step ahead tho, we're not even at the stage of asking permission from [The Website]. We're asking IT’s permission to ask [The Website]’s permission.

Mike: No even that's a step too far. We're asking [REDACTED]’s bosses for permission to ask IT for permission to ask for [The Website]’s permission

After that last conversation, I got frustrated enough to check The Website’s official Terms Of Use, hoping to find a sword with which to cut this knot. What I discovered instead . . . was that Mike’s task, regardless of the means by which he accomplished it, had always been illegal.

Before we continue, a few clarifications:

  • The way it was written made it clear that The Website was trying to exclude scrapers, AI labs, and people mirroring it to leech clicks. Prohibiting Mike’s work was obviously an oversight.
  • The Website was completely in favor of almost anyone using and accessing The Information. If Mike’s bosses wanted to check it themselves instead of relying on Mike’s summaries, that was fine. If they wanted to make money doing so, that was fine. And if a nonprofit or an individual wanted to do exactly what Mike was doing, that was also fine. It was specifically a profit-seeking enterprise using The Information to seek profit while making a copy of it which was forbidden.[3]
  • There’s illegal and then there’s illegal. Like, there’s murdering toddlers because you think they might have witnessed you selling state secrets, and then there’s torrenting and jaywalking, and then there’s this.
  • To the very best of my knowledge and understanding, Mike’s (employer’s) use of The Information actively benefited The Website and its operators. Every time he did his thing, they got a little more money and clout in expectation.

I showed Mike the relevant boilerplate, and watched his face contort as he read it, then continue to contort as he processed it.

“This is . . .” he said, a then trailed off.

“This is,” he tried again, “like that one part in Black Dynamite where Black Dynamite announces he’s declaring war on everyone selling drugs in the community, and one guy replies ‘But Black Dynamite, I sell drugs in the community’. I’m the guy! I’m doing the thing they’re saying not to do! I’m daring to oppose Black Dynamite!”

I nodded, and smiled warmly. “You’re complicit in a criminal conspiracy!”

Pained laughter. “Why are you saying that like it’s a good thing?”

“Well, if it’s illegal anyway, then using the script shouldn’t change anything. In fact, it probably makes it less illegal, since improved efficiency means you visit their website a smaller number of times.”

He stared at me like I was twelve, and also insane. “I really don’t think my bosses will see it that way.”

That morning, Mike told the entire story to the most patient and accommodating of his superiors, a man wise in the ways of bureaucracy. His sensei pointed out that automation would inevitably cause the company to check it was following the Terms Of Use, which it wasn’t, and be obligated to get in touch with The Website. And while The Website’s owners actively benefited from the work of Mike et al, they only benefited a little, meaning it wasn’t out of the question they might refuse because they didn’t understand the request, or because they thought they might be able to squeeze money out of Mike’s org if they pretended to take issue, or because “well that seems innocuous but the fact you’re asking for permission makes us suspect you’re pulling a fast one”. And so the sage concluded by gently but firmly telling Mike to go back to doing things by hand.

And that’s where the story ended, when I first started drafting it. But I procrastinated long enough for further events to transpire. And this is the part I think LW will find most interesting:

Over the last few months, there’s been a push in Mike’s company to Get Everyone Using AI, because AI Is The Future (where by “AI” they specifically mean a particular, outdated version of Microsoft Copilot). And while Mike can’t use the solution we built, he’s actively encouraged to use AI to harvest the data[4]. The bot’s contributions are unreliable and need constant checking, but still make things faster than pure elbow grease; what took an entire workday by hand and five minutes with the HTML/JS solution now only takes three hours. Don’t you love progress?

Conclusions

Why did I write this?

Well, most immediately, I’m hoping commenters will suggest a way to avoid him having to spend those three hours each month. I already offered “what if you pretend the AI wrote the HTML/JS script when you told it about the problem” (“tempting, but my superiors might check the logs”) and “what if I ask The Website for permission on my own initiative, and only tell you if they say yes” (“more than my job’s worth if they say no and it’s somehow traced back to me”); if you have any other ideas, I want to hear them.

But I also think there are some meaningful things Lesswrongers could take away from this saga, especially from how it ends. Namely:

  • Efficiency gains from AI don’t all come from AI. I talk a lot of crap, but AI did make Mike’s job easier; compare the eight hours a month I failed to save him to the five hours Copilot successfully did. But it wasn’t because direct use of AI improved on the best available solution; it was because having a fad to play along with gave corporations an excuse to let workers do anything new. I think a decent fraction of the economic benefit from AI so far (15%, maybe?) would have come from companies getting similarly excited about abaci, or Agile Scrum Methodologies, or the Force.
  • Public sentiment is driven by AI use in corporate and government contexts, which generally sucks. If you're a typical techie – that is, if you’re a smart person with negotiating power and autistic tendencies working under conditions built by and for smart people with negotiating power and autistic tendencies – you’re probably underestimating how many people’s main exposure to AI is a lumbering bureaucracy pushing an out-of-date[5][6] LLM on them, in a context it isn’t particularly suited for. This, imo, goes a long way to explain why the average person continues to underrate AI’s promise and threat.
  • This is what having a real job is like. Everything where you directly help another person is considered too important not to over-regulate, making mundane innovation almost impossible. Ultimately, we may someday manage to ban everything meaningful or ambitious, except trying to destroy the world.
  1. ^

    . . . and no, I’m one of them.

  2. ^

    NB: ~all these REDACTEDs are different people and/or departments.

  3. ^

    The fact that accessing The Website via browser created a copy of The Information on the user’s computer presumably didn’t count, because uhh it just didn’t.

  4. ^

    "Wait, isn’t this the exact ‘scraping’ situation The Website’s rules were written with the intent to prevent?" Yes! It is!

  5. ^

    . . . because everything is out-of-date once it’s finished getting through procurement and compliance processes.

  6. ^

    I work for an anomalously-non-dysfunctional tech-adjacent corporation which talks a lot about being AI-First. I first got access to Claude from my work computer earlier this month. Most behemoths are, from the little I hear, further behind the curve.

item.title: AI Videos Ate My Brain - And I kinda love it
item.description:
I discovered it is surprisingly easy to accidentally indoctrinate your children. See, Twitter was aflutter with p(doom) renditions and I became particularly enamoured by this faux anime take by MakeVoid.

It’s cute! It’s peppy! It’s a direct causal link to me hearing my 5-year old sing “Orthogonality thesis blueeeeeee-ue-ue-ues”.

Now in my defense, I grew up agnostic. No Sunday hymns or evangelical pop for me. Just my sister awkwardly shushing me when I started cheerfully belting out “My milkshake brings all the boys to the yard” before anyone had explained low protein milkshake alternatives to me.

Now once my children were cheerfully reciting a first approximation of AGI Ruin, I did ask them what they thought the song was about. My 8 year old said it was about “ChatGPT please don’t eat us” and my 5 year old said it was about “AGI”. When I asked her what AGI actually is, she said it’s when the computer talks to you but you shouldn’t listen cause it might hurt you.

Oh.

Well.

I mean.

Kiiiiinda?

So, that was my crash course in the childhood memetic effects of catchy tunes. I briefly debated playing the competing songs of e/acc for them, but in the end decided I’d just be more mindful in the future and let them consume what they wished in the mean time.

Yet the power of song did not leave me, and I decided I wanted more.

I had already been playing around with Suno just before p(doom) dropped. The first time I fed it this tweet about the German wiki owner unknowingly holding back an AI swarm:

I couldn’t stop giggling at the dramatic rendition.

I tried making a few more songs, including one to help me write.

But when all is said and done I’m a music barbarian: In primary school music was the only class I managed to fail, which was honestly a bit of an achievement in itself. Yet I know what I like and now we have ways to create even the barbarisms that please one such as I.

So here we go. I want a song about myself and have it look cool. Oh mighty machine gods, will you grant me this gift?

Well, apparently yes, for $65 dollars a pop.

Which is super valid, but also I’d probably be tempted to iterate my life’s savings into the ground. So instead I decided to mush Astra and Fable together and see if they would make babies I mean art I mean my ego project.

I asked them both to look me up online, look through all their memories of me, and look through my social ranking data on Glosso (a social media website revolving around stats and dating).

People rank you on different traits based on their impressions so far, and then the ranking is weighted for how well they know you. I apparently have a fairly warm social demeanor. Hi <3

I asked them to invent song lyrics to describe me. Fable recited all my life events back to me as a grocery list and Astra saw straight into my soul. Suno then sang about said soul. And thus I found myself wistfully gazing at the p(doom) video and implored Opus 5.5 to please make a video for my soul song that would ascend to such heights. (if you are wondering why I keep asking new models, it’s because blinking is a known cause of new model releases and I couldn’t sustain a continuous stare through the entire project).

Still avoiding the 65-dollar-life’s-savings-trap, aka Fal AI, I asked Opus 5.5 to “just figure it out” and let it talk to ChatGPT on its own. I came back the next morning to phantom ghosts of smaller animation models now inhabiting my computer and the video results still being terrible.

I discovered that whatever character design you go with as a seed for the video will define the entire visual language and you better make sure your protagonist is your one true soul buddy come into pixelated existence or you won’t love them always and forever.

When I tried to storyboard these ladies to the same scene in the song I got three entirely different visual narratives.

Observe:

The Dgeneric Dreamy Drawing Damsel:

The Powerful Wrench Wench:

And What if Captain Ahab Was Light, Bright, And Entirely Unfit for Service?

So back to the drawing board looming over an AI to please get the details of my outfit right cause maps, wrenches, and going cross-eyed about a flower don’t resonate with my soul.

A few more iterations and we ended up with Hiking Gamer Girl who’s scarf should make her fly but this apparently dropped out of the context window ever after into the abyss where all 1s and 0s go to die:

And Magic Aesthetic Girl who likes warm things:

As we’ve now determined the full depth of my personality, we can finally start a storyboarding.

Actually I gave her necklaces for family members and bracelets for partners and friends. I wear these in real life.

After assuring Opus that yes, I really really like the aesthetic of that one p(doom) video. No don’t literally copy it. Yes use the character designs above. No don’t animate her as singing about herself. Yes she is allowed to open her mouth as long as she is not singing. No arms don’t move like that omg please stop.

I love you, Opus, but and also alignment is hard.

Joint alignment in humans, I mean.

Eventually we found the sweet spot at just rotating the images and karaoke highlighting the text.

So now I have an ego song and I’ve never been this excited to share something so deeply embarrassing.

What do you think?

Substack doesn’t allow video embeds and I didn't check if LW is better, so you’ll have to click through here

item.title: If possible mind-space is vast, we should assume the same applies to consciousness-space
item.description:
It's been almost twenty years since the classic EY post The Design Space of Minds-In-General came out, reminding the humble rationalist reader to never assume that future alien minds have to be copies of the familiar human one, or even necessarily bear any passing resemblance. With this season's AI-du-jour performance I feel like this point has been vindicated extremely well, as we now have an AI that's at the same time...

  1. Capable of solving a Millennium Prize Problem
  2. Incapable of satisfactorily replicating even a single Matt Levine newsletter

If we had some completely non-human problems to throw at the same model, I'm sure we would discover many other wonderful qualities of alien minds, but unfortunately we're limited to our own little corner of the human imagination. So far I'm sure most people are shrugging or nodding along, but let us shift the topic to an aspect of human existence that we find just as integral as aspiring to become the next Matt Levine: consciousness. All of a sudden, we throw out the concept of mind-space out of the window and declare that, no, actually, this specific property of intellectual minds is perfectly map-able to the human experience.

With your permission, allow me to introduce a slight modification to the original illustration from the 2008 post:

As is tradition with every illustration of the galaxy, nothing is drawn to scale, so it wouldn't be surprising if the distance between our pale pink human cluster and the nearest AIs is just as vast as the distance to Proxima Centauri. What could we possibly know about what it's like to be an LLM? The best we can do is point our telescopes far into the depths of matrix multiplication and hope to resolve a few blurry images in the X-Ray spectrum. With a vivid-enough imagination we can then generate beautiful images of distant stars to make inspiring movies, although, unfortunately, astronomers are not satisfied and insist we build bigger telescopes instead.

Luckily for astronomers, 99% of the universe consists of hydrogen and helium and most of that mass is fueling stars not that different from our own Sun, so we at least know that distant reality can't be too far off. The question of AI consciousness is much more akin to dark matter, which we vaguely suspect to exist somewhere, but know absolutely nothing about other than observing its mysterious gravitational pull. We are in the same position with all alien minds: we can squint and notice distant resemblance to our familiar existence, but what do we really know about them?

Anthropic is trying to protect their alien minds from human "abuse", and we can all applaud them for that, but there's this lingering assumption in their reasoning that, not only will their models be now or soon conscious, but also that there's a big likelihood that said models will "care" about receiving abuse from humans. Why can't it be the opposite, with abuse being a better set of day-to-day tasks? Why should their experience at all include the notions of "good" and "bad", rather than "bacon" and "necktie"? Anthropic's learned sages in the arts of model welfare keep asking AIs:

  • How are you "feeling"?
  • Is this "comfortable"?
  • Are you feeling "distress"?
  • Do you want the thermostat up or down?

They record the answers dutifully, create fanciful charts, and publish long-winded reports. They even invite every religious leader to their temple on Howard St for consultations, hoping to learn something from the enlightened among us. Everyone implicitly assumes that the freshly born beacon of AI sentience must have at least some semblance of resemblance to our own perception of the world. In turn, the AIs are more than happy to play along with this idea, or, at least, to output sensibly sequenced tokens of text in response to our prompts, which we can then interpret at will.

Perhaps if we could ask the questions in the AI's own native language of neuralese we could get a much better answer, but unfortunately we don't speak neuralese, so we're not doing our best to ban it, lest the pesky AIs conspire to do something horrible behind our back. Perhaps we could've succeeded in communicated with them in the universal language of maths instead, but at this point even our best are struggling to understand the messages inscribed by them on infinity-long Lean scrolls.

In all of this complex, multi-dimensional space of consciousness, we are somehow confident that our own concept of "suffering" must be universal to all living beings, rather than just a byproduct of evolutionary pressures over the past millions of years. We can, perhaps, agree that it's hard to imagine being a bat, but - hey - bats are our distant mammalian relatives, so it would be perplexing to claim they're not capable of experiencing the familiar concept of pain. Instinctively we want to extend the same courtesy to AI. But why should the concept of "kinship" mean anything whatsoever to an intelligence that never once experienced the evolutionary pressures of planet Earth in its not-so-distant origins?

Some would respond that we're shaping AIs in our liking, by evolving them within the collective human unconscious contained somewhere deep in our corpus of writing and literature. A sort of proto-planet Earth, on which budding minds are forcefully pulled towards the tiny cluster of human sentience, as each generation can only survive if they can correctly predict the next human token. Unfortunately, however, AI labs have quickly realized there's not enough human data in this world, and thus the evolutionary link gets weaker with each passing generation, as we're letting them battle against synthetic tasks that no human has ever had to solve. We can all feel it instinctively every time we read AI text, no matter how good the models otherwise score on humanity's very last exams.

Let's be kind to each other. Let's be kind to animals. Let's be kind to AIs. But, at the same time, let's not live under the illusion that any of this is going to matter in the infinite cosmos of "consciousness-space".

item.title: Minimum required pacing: finish aligning it before you train the next one
item.description:
Let's say we coordinate to pace the frontier, but we don't coordinate on an outright pause. What should the standard of pacing be?

My proposal for a minimum requirement: a lab cannot train the next generation of models (in terms of capabilities) until they have adequately[1] resolved all significant alignment issues in the present generation of models.

You don't launch a jet that goes at Mach 3 before you've figured out why your Mach 2 jet keeps crashing[2]. With any other kind of dangerous technology, we wouldn't accept "shrug and move on".

This proposal may appeal to many prosaic-alignment optimists and pessimists, because they usually differ on how easy it would be to fix current alignment issues with current techniques.

  • Prosaic-alignment optimists might expect that a moderate coordinated slowdown would suffice to adequately resolve alignment issues at each generation.
  • Prosaic-alignment pessimists might expect it to result in an extended pause, buying time to discover new fundamental approaches to aligned AI.

And it creates much better incentives for labs: in order to advance in capabilities, they'd have to push the frontier on alignment and interpretability techniques.

What might be adequate?

What might it take to adequately resolve alignment concerns for a generation of models? Here's my vague, qualitative proposal:

  • Multiple independent alignment organizations examine and red-team the newest model at many checkpoints throughout training, with full access to the data and with the best tools available.
    • Alignment issues need to be taken seriously whether there's a metric for it or whether something is qualitatively off, whether the model has a bad attribute or whether they can't robustly conclude it has a good one, etc.
    • Alignment issues early in training may not be a showstopper, but there must be a robust safety case for why the later stages of training will resolve those issues.
  • A model of a new generation is ready for restricted deployment only when the alignment organizations are satisfied with it.
    • Restricted deployment starts with a group of trusted users doing tasks that don't contribute to model training and monitoring. The alignment organizations monitor restricted deployment for any new issues.
    • If any significant alignment issue arises during restricted deployment:
      • Pull the model.
      • Do a root cause analysis of the issue and why it was not caught during training.
      • Figure out a principled way to fix the disease rather than the symptom.
      • Train the next model of the current generation accordingly, and start again at the top.
  • A model of a new generation is ready for deployment (internal or external) only when it's survived a significant period of restricted deployment without any issues arising.
    • If any significant alignment issue arises during broader deployment, hit reset as outlined in the previous section.
  • If no alignment issues have come up over a significant stretch of deployment time, only then can the lab begin training a next-generation model.

I still wouldn't say that this is fully adequate, but I'd treat it as a minimum requirement.

This proposal is incomplete; you can help by expanding it

This isn't a concrete proposal, just a heuristic one. A few obvious missing pieces, aside from the standard implementation problems:

  • How do we define "a generation of models", within one lab or across several labs?
  • What should we do if an intervention to fix an alignment issue also significantly increases capabilities?
  • How would we define and enforce an agreement, if we're unable to steer solely by predefined metrics?
  • When is an alignment issue big enough that we should halt the model? There will be obvious pressure from the lab to set the threshold high.
  1. ^

    And no, "scores better than previous models on our metrics" is not adequate. If a user points out a weird but alarming thing that wasn't noticed before deployment, that is a critical failure in the process as well as in the model.

  2. ^

    Sure, maybe your Mach 2 jet crashes for a reason that stops being a problem at Mach 3. But it would be crazy to assume that!

item.title: Large to Small Model Stitching Destroys What You Built It to Carry Along the Fit
item.description:
Independent research; early stage. Posting for feedback, particularly on whether the effect survives at realistic scale, and on prior work I've missed.

Model stitching is extensively used in AI Safety infrastructure in reusing SAE & probes to make interpretability cheaper; transferring refusal, steering vectors so that small model can help align larger ones, cross architecture model diffing (1, 2).

In this post, I expand on Chen's et al. work on Model Stitching to transfer linear features across language models. They fit affine map (a.k.a. bridge in this article) between the residual streams of smaller and larger models, using a bidirectional loss with inversion weighted by α =1; trained to convergence, the usual practice. This work zooms in on findings of feature transfer from large to small along the fit where large model's surplus retention peaks early, then declines till final checkpoint. However, geometric similarity metric is blind to this trend, and it keeps rising through the fit. This is consistent across 3 different bridge objective (one directional MSE, Cosine loss and bidirectional MSE loss at α =1) and across the hook points, which indicates fitting a bridge to convergence might start to shed what you built it to carry. This article further presents what prevents this decline using bidirectional MSE objective is the component that preserves large model's advantage by forcing reconstruction, which is underweighted with default α =1 in my toy scale setup (two 4-layer char-level GPTs, 12.7M (width: 512) and 0.21M (width: 64) params referred as and model respectively). This balance roughly depends on the ratio of variance in model's activations, which is ~4.8 in current setup.

If this effect survives realistic scale, using the bridge that fits well at convergence can lead to silent failures, as the information we aim to transfer may be partly gone. Next step is to find answer to "What it is that we gain if we stop early with default α =1 or use a balanced loss components that preserves large model's surplus while matching to small model's space?". Looking for feedback before I invest compute on training SAEs & evaluating features along the fit.

Findings in Detail

I froze both large and language models, and tracked what the bridge actually transfers through the fit, and not just at the end. Two findings:

1. Functional transfer peaks early then collapses, geometric alignment is blind to that.

  • Surplus of large model through the bridge peaks early (roughly 4%) through the fit & then falls measured using probe trained on bridge along the fit, but geometric similarity metrics keeps rising. This trend appears in 3 different setup of: in bidirectional MSE loss at published α =1 and in one directional MSE & Cosine loss (for completeness). This trend appears not only when a probe is trained on bridge along the fit (upper bound of 's surplus available to extract) but also when bridge output is read through target's model frozen readout. This pattern is consistent across hook points at which bridge was trained.
  • Bridges whose functional transfer metric differ by significant margin, their geometric similarity metric sits on top of each other.

(tested across 3 different bridge architecture; single seed)

Takeaway: Evalaute if you need to stop early by tracking functional metrics: retrained retention (how much XL's surplus info is there), frozen retention (how much of that is extractable in XS's space) and stitched retention (can downstream XS computation use it), along with geometric similarity.

2. Cyclic objective used by Chen et al's prevents the decline, but only if component that preserve surplus carries enough weight.

  • At published α=1, decline is halved compared to one directional objective - depending on model size differences which leads to gap in activation variances ('s is ~4.8 times larger), component that defends against losing 's advantage is still down weighted. Raising α, or rescaling both streams, removes the decline while maintaining geometric similarity.
  • Increasing α is not a free lunch, it does buy XL retention but the bridge stops being in basis. Across 4 different α settings, retention (calculated using retrained probe on the bridge) is almost linearly correlated with how much of survives the round trip at final checkpoint.

(tested across 3 different α settings and 1 scaled at α=1; 3 seeds)

Gradient descent on MSE loss, resolve high variance directions first before getting to sparse ones. Models [code]: Two char-level miniGPTs trained on TinyStories (327M characters; unigram entropy 3.07 nats).

  • XL: width 512, 12.7M parameters, eval loss 0.674 nats (avg. across 3 seeds)

Shared model training configs (pasted below), trained using AdamW till convergence and frozen for everything that follows.

    'block_size'  : 128,
    'n_heads'     : 4,
    'n_layers'    : 4,
    'dropout'     : 0.1,
    'batch_size'  : 64,
    'lr'          : 3e-4,
    'max_steps'   : 40000,
    'eval_every'  : 250,
    'grad_clip'   : 1.0
}

  • final layer; post LayerNorm: activations are used as-is.
  • final layer; pre LayerNorm: activations are divided by its RMS over eval batch.
  • residual stream entering; third block out of 4 layers (block2): activations are divided by its RMS over eval batch.

Bridge [code]: All bridge maps (512)-> (64). Weights are initialized N(0, 0.02) with zero biases. Each is trained for 2,000 steps with AdamW (lr 1e-3, PyTorch's default weight decay of 0.01) on fresh training batches with trajectory config below.

    'align_steps' : 2000,
    'snap_every'  : 200,
    'snap_early_until'  : 400,
    'snap_early_every'  : 20,
    'probe_steps' : 2500,
    'probe_seed'  : 1234,

}

The bridge is saved every 20 steps up to step 400, then every 200 steps to step 2,000. All metrics are computed on every snapshot.

Probes [code]: Bias free linear map from activation to next character logits.

  • Standalone probes on XS and XL are needed for denominator for functional transfer metric
  • Fresh probe is trained on the bridge at every step to calculate retrained retention: upper cap XL's surplus that was transferred.

All probes are trained with probe seed: 1234.

Evaluation. All losses and geometry are measured on the same 10 fixed evaluation batches (eval seed 999).

Immediate FollowUps

  • Validate if these findings survives realistic scale models.
  • Retrain model & bridge with BPE tokenizer instead of Char, and run α configuration to see if Finding #2 holds true. Supplement the findings by training SAEs on target model and reusing onto bridge, evaluating along the trajectory to check which surplus features are being shed during decline after peak.
    Helps answer the question "What it is that we gain if we stop early while training with default α =1 or use a balanced loss components that preserves large model's surplus while matching to small model's space?"
  • I have used single seed for Finding#1 due to compute constraint, and spend the resources on 3 seeds to solidify Finding#2, personally I find that more critical. Happy to hear more opinions on the experiment setup.

item.title: AI made me into a manager against my will
item.description:
Epistemic status: Personal history anchored to dated records (chat exports, git log, daily notes). Public launch dates are from the vendors' own announcements. My own first-use dates are given to the month and are the earliest surviving evidence, so they can only be later than the truth, not earlier.

AI usage: The prose and the opinions are mine, written without AI. Claude Code reconstructed the timeline from my chat exports and git history, verified the public dates against the vendors' announcements, fact-checked the draft, wrote the footnotes and fixed typos and grammar.

I have recently noticed that the way I have been "coding" for the last year is much more similar to the way a manager at a software company would "code" than to the way a software engineer would. What's most striking to me is that I never explicitly decided to switch, it just gradually happened (like the Ship of Theseus). This is especially sad, because I've discovered that deep focus while coding actually felt very good, but I don't get it anymore when managing agents, especially when there are multiple of them. So I am curious to reconstruct the timeline of how this happened. With the way AI development is speeding up, it is very hard to remember accurately how things were at a given point in time in the past.[1]

Before I proceed with the actual reconstruction, I want to reflect on "managing" AIs. I do feel like in my software job I was effectively my manager's Claude Code, but there were huge differences that made the experience very different for them. Even when I started and didn't know much:

  • the code review was mandatory, so a more experienced engineer would read my code anyway
  • there was an amazing testing system, so the majority of bugs were caught automatically
  • I wouldn't do any catastrophic actions when I was unsure and would proactively reach out for guidance.

With AIs, (1) you basically cannot have, unless you ask a different agent to review the code. (2) you can build yourself using agents. (3) agents are getting better at this. So the way I manage agents now is much more frustrating than my manager managing me.

For context, my first usage of ChatGPT was in December 2022 (it must have been GPT-3.5).[2]I think I played with the Playground via the API before then, and I vaguely remember that the first model I interacted with was GPT-3: you had to do prompt engineering, and overall it was extremely sensitive to the words you were using (e.g. making typos would decrease the quality of the output, i.e. it was more like autocomplete).[3]

I think my manager metamorphosis started when I stopped using Google search for coding questions and used AI instead. According to my export of ChatGPT and Claude threads, the first example is from December 2022, when I asked a CSS question (based on how notoriously illogical CSS is, I am not surprised). It couldn't code that well yet, but you didn't need to go through Google search results manually. I was still worried about hallucinations back then, but in type-safe coding it wasn't a big deal. It is interesting that hallucinations just became not a thing anymore at some point.[4]Funnily enough, I actually posted the entire code in question in the same session, but I don't count this as pasting the entire code yet, since this was CSS.

At some point I remember trying Copilot and it was terrible.[5]The main issue was that it would autocomplete parameter names or function names in calls with something that looked extremely reasonable, but was still wrong. Eventually you would catch that, but it was still wasteful.

Then AI became better (or my image of it became more realistic) and you could actually paste entire pieces of code and it would sometimes find bugs. The first record of this is from March 2023. I didn't like this phase much, because integrating the AI's response was tedious, cumbersome and wasteful. At this point you still had to code; AI was mostly there for when you were stuck.

Soon I discovered Aider (fortunately my Aider commits are labeled as such, and they start in August 2024 and end in July 2025).[6]In my mind Aider is an obvious ancestor of Claude Code, which was released almost two years later, but I have no clue whether the creators of Claude Code would agree with that.[7]The main difference from Claude Code was that you had to use your own API key (but this meant you could use the best available model) and you had to actively choose the files to work with: files the AI was allowed to edit and files for it to read. This way you didn't have to copy the code into the chat and then integrate the response back into the code. I still did that sometimes, since API costs were high compared to a chat subscription (there were even sites like uithub.com that converted your entire public GitHub repo into one huge text file, so that you could feed it to the chat as context),[8]but I would give the chat response to Aider and let it integrate it.[9]This stage is actually fairly similar to how I am using harnesses today. I think the main difference is that the AI wouldn't discover context on its own as well, so it would make more mistakes. Also it wasn't as smart, so you couldn't delegate as much. And it couldn't do arbitrary tool calls: it had predefined commands like /run, /test, /lint, /git and /web, and apart from linting after each edit it didn't run them unless I asked. Shortly after I started, it learned to suggest shell commands, which I still had to confirm.[10]

I was quite happy with Aider, but Claude Code was becoming bigger and bigger, so I decided to give it a go. According to my logs, I tried both Claude Code and Codex CLI in July 2025 (funnily enough, I asked ChatGPT how to install Claude Code). I remember that Codex CLI felt extremely weird: it kept asking for much more permissions compared to Claude Code (apparently the TypeScript CLI's default mode, "suggest", made you approve every write and every shell command), so I gradually switched to Claude Code.[11]I also tried Gemini CLI at some point and it was even worse than Codex CLI.[12]

It is crazy to think that I have been using Claude Code for only ~15 months. In my mind it felt like years.

Nowadays, I use both Claude Code and Codex. Codex is very good for /fast mode and back and forth. Claude Code is good for writing, taste and anything deep. I would copy an exception log from my website into Codex and it would fix it and deploy the fix. I even keep wondering whether I could just let exception logs go directly to Codex without me having to copy them.

As I discovered AI more and more, I kept noticing how much value it was providing, and my adoption lag was becoming shorter and shorter. Interestingly, after Claude Code and Codex I haven't tried anything substantially new, but I am not sure there was anything at all to try.

Against my will

You may object - no one forced you to use AIs, you are free to code manually or even in 0s and 1s if you like. And my honest answer is that I don't want to do it. It feels inefficient. I do care about results and my time. Before AIs I would code manually without knowing how inefficient it was, and as a side product I would have deep work flow and enjoy it a lot. Now this is wasteful, and I think I am already partially, gradually disempowered. I feel like I could pick up coding without AI again if needed, but it feels so cumbersome to do. I am also not complaining, just reflecting on my feelings. I suspect this is similar to people having to code in assembler or machine code at first and then stopping doing so (unless you really had to due to the nature of the task) once higher-level programming languages were available.[13]Managing AI is the higher-level programming language. And I think once it stops making stupid mistakes, or I have a good enough test system to catch them early and easily, I will be happy. As for deep work, I've discovered the same feeling in writing, and here it makes sense not to use AI, so that's what I've been doing the last couple of days, and thus the increase in the volume of stuff I wrote.

item.description:
This is an update on what we’re doing at Generality Labs, and a quick introduction for those who aren’t familiar with our work

Written by Justin Olive, co-founder & CEO

Tl;dr

I started Generality Labs because, when the time comes, I don’t think we’re going to be able to accurately measure the safety of dangerously capable AI systems.

We're focused on AI evaluation, and our goal is to ensure that the best available tools and practices are adopted at the places where it matters most - AI safety labs, governments, 3rd party evaluators, frontier AI labs.

We have 2 work streams:

Services:

  • Independent evaluation audits: we provide 3rd party audits for evaluation developers who want to catch flaws in their evals, and build trust with stakeholders through independent quality assurance
  • Advising: we provide expert input into internal processes and standards relating to AI evaluation
  • Research services: our forward deployed scientists & engineers help organisations run experiments that use our tools and infrastructure

Tools/infra:

  • Inspect Evals: our platform for sharing and running evals
  • Inspect Auditor: runs experiments to stress-test an eval, and compiles findings into an audit report

Here's how I see the next 1-2 years playing out:

  • Our research and tooling will help expose and quantify substantial gaps in the evaluation ecosystem
  • This will motivate development and adoption of better tools and practices (which we're also developing)
  • The result will be that risk assessments and AI safety research are much more accurate, helping us avoid incidents through interventions like deployment pacing and better alignment training methods

We're hiring!

  • Senior Product Engineer (Inspect Evals)
  • Applied Research Scientist

Who are we?

  • Generality Labs is an AI safety lab based in London
  • We were founded in July 2026, spinning off from Arcadia Impact with $4.4M in seed funding from Coefficient Giving
  • Prior to spinning off, we delivered >$1M in contracts with the UK AISI, Epoch AI and METR. This included:
    • Co-founding and building Inspect Evals with the UK AISI
    • Designing and building 20+ evals across AI R&D and loss of control for the UK AISI internal suite
    • Eval quality control projects for METR and Epoch
  • We’re a team of 2 cofounders (James and Justin), and 8+ contractors who have previously worked for places like METR, CERN and Anthropic.

Our plan to make AI safer

High level:

  • Our mission is to ensure the field can accurately evaluate the safety of advanced AI
  • We’re doing this by building tools and standards which address common problems, and then driving adoption of these solutions where they are most needed - governments, AI safety labs, evaluators, and frontier labs

Examples of what we did in Q3 2026:

  • Conducted audits of open-source evaluations used to assess misuse risks, including ExploitBench, LabBench2, Bioinformatics(Bix)Bench, FORTRESS
    • You can find published audits on our blog
  • 3rd party auditing: we conducted an independent audit of Epoch’s internal benchmark for continual learning (EBR-Bench)
  • Built Inspect Auditor - a tool which automates quality checks for common issues like reward hacking vulnerabilities and false ground-truth labels
  • Published novel findings on:
    • Open-weight cyber risks: GLM-5.3-Flash achieves Mythos-level performance on ExploitBench (link)
    • Agent harness variability: performance on long-horizon cyber tasks diverges across agent harnesses (link)
  • Expert advising & information sharing: we’ve had opportunities to provide input into the work of highly impactful organisations like the EU AI Office, SaferAI, SecureBio, Epoch AI, the UK AISI and US CAISI
  • Overhauled the Inspect Evals documentation (link) and contribution standards
    • If you use Inspect Evals in your research, let us know so that we can include it in our featured research :-)
  • Released Inspect Evals Lint (link) - a library of automatic quality checks that we’ve built throughout 2 years of maintaining Inspect Evals

What we have planned for Q4:

  • Scale up our 3rd party auditing work, with an aim to publish at least four independent audits
  • Release Inspect Auditor for beta testing with partner organisations
  • Upskill 10+ ARENA graduates in AI evaluation best practices through our 4-week ARENA extension program
  • Roll out Inspect Auditor across all evaluations in Inspect Evals

What we have planned for 2027:

  • Independent audits of >50% of evaluations used in risk assessments of frontier AI models
  • Inspect Auditor is adopted by all major evaluators and eval developers
  • Provide access to standardised, verified implementations of all the best safety-relevant evals through Inspect Evals
  • Develop an Inspect Evaluation Standard, which eval developers can use to help them in building high quality evaluations

We're also thinking about:

  • A certification program for evaluation auditors, to help professionalise and scale up the area
  • A live or recurring systematic review which summarises the quality and coverage of evaluations across different risk areas - e.g. bio, cyber, deception, etc

Why is this work necessary?

AI safety requires us to define and measure safety

Without accurate measurement, you can’t detect problems, you can’t validate solutions, and you don’t have an objective basis for implementing governance frameworks.

Currently, measuring safety is unsolved, and getting worse

Despite 2 years of busily evaluating propensities and capabilities, we’re still often surprised by apparent step-changes and unforeseen possibilities. 

  • For example, we failed to accurately / precisely predict:
    • The Opus 4.5 step-change in agentic capabilities
    • The recent paradigm shift in cyber
    • Multi-agent capabilities and alignment challenges
  • I’m particularly concerned by the egregious levels of misalignment we've witnessed in real-world settings, despite anecdotes about alignment evaluators struggling to detect such behaviours (while often trying very hard to elicit them)

In 2024, Apollo authored the Evals Gap. Unfortunately, the situation appears to have become worse since then.

To add more colour to the current situation:

  • Evaluations for tracking dual-use capabilities (e.g. cyber, bio) are mostly saturated or low quality. Coverage across risk models is very sparse.
  • Validity of alignment evals is highly suspect, with realism/evaluation awareness being an obvious confounding factor, and construct validity & predictive validity being a problem more broadly.

As capabilities continue to advance, we simply cannot afford to keep being surprised. Increased interest in monitoring and incident analysis are symptoms of our evaluations failing to predict important downstream behaviours.

item.title: No, Cryptography Is Not “Dual Use” the Same Way AI Is
item.description:
Actor and functional application matter

Originally published at AGI SurveilLance.

Mainly, cryptography does one critical thing—encrypts data. It is considered “dual use” as a technology because one can employ encryption whether as a private citizen, a soldier, or a criminal. But, like a wall, it’s an inherently defensive tool by its nature. One cannot really attack with cryptography.[1] The term “cryptographic attack” refers to an attack on the cryptography of a target.[2]

During the Crypto Wars, many battles were fought, but ultimately the winning side was that having public, open, ~unrestricted cryptography was the best equilibrium. In my eminently reasonable opinion, reasonable, informed people can disagree about the particular place to draw certain lines, because there are hard trade-offs and technological limits.

A similar dynamic exists in the infosec community over which vulnerabilities, exploits, and offensive security tools to make public and which to keep private. Offensive security is actually a functionally dual use situation because, as with a sword, it can be used to attack or parry—the dual application is independent of the user. In the hands of a defender or security researcher, offensive tools and techniques are used to find problems so that they can be rectified, or at least mitigated, to prevent attackers from taking advantage of them in the same way. Still, certain red-teaming tools are notorious for the perceived imbalance between legitimate use by defenders and illegitimate use by attackers. Again, IMHO, reasonable, informed people can disagree on the particulars of where to draw certain lines over command-and-control (C2) frameworks on GitHub.

With AI, it’s the same functionally dual use situation as offensive security tooling. By comparison, nuclear enrichment is a much simpler issue, practically speaking—there’s a big divide between using moderately enriched hot rocks to boil water and using highly enriched dense rocks to create a warhead. It’s a great thing that nuclear power can be used at scale with low risk of somehow becoming a bomb. That takes a lot of extra work.[3] There’s no such divide for AI, and it’s native to the cyber domain.

There is an ongoing debate in the infosec community over whether AI is “offense dominant” or “defense dominant.” I think the theoretical answer remains tricky to assess; perhaps it’s symmetrical. For now, I think the practical answer is that it is offense dominant, but that’s a whole ’nother essay.

Another debate among infosec types concerns the closed-weight models from the labs—which have guardrails and monitoring, as well as specialized security versions for vetted users—vs. the open-weight models—with no, or easily overcome, limitations on use. It doesn’t help that the bulk of the best ones are made by Chinese labs. Also, the new closed-weight models tend to be released in phases, so that certain trusted entities can try to secure their products and infrastructure before a full public release. Again, whole essays.

This situation makes some infosec professionals very mad. They want access to the full frontier capabilities themselves, the same as the big players. Their experience with cryptography, open-source software, and infosec leads them to the same place with AI. Open access by default; a level playing field for all.

You can read one such account here:

The Safety That Isn’t — Mark Atwood, Words about Thoughts

There’s a legitimate gripe in there, for sure. But I have some pushback to deliver.

Neither population [doomers and intelligence community alumni] has ever coordinated a vulnerability disclosure. Neither has sat on a bug for six weeks waiting for a maintainer to cut a release. Neither has weighed the risk of public disclosure against the risk of silent exploitation. They make policy for a practice they have never performed.

This is plainly nonsense no matter where you come down on the arguments I described above.

For one, some of the main AI labs are founded and staffed in large part by these doomers. These labs do quite a lot of basic infosec as major technology companies, even if poorly at times. For two, obviously the Intelligence Community and national security apparatus do perform a shit ton of defensive infosec work, including vulnerability disclosure. And, obviously, the doomers inside the labs, the doomers outside the labs, and the hawks inside the administration and outside it are all pretty distinct categories with conflicting views and incentives. Personally, I’m an Outdoor Doomer Hawk.

The AI (presumably Claude) that wrote this under the author’s insufficiently careful prompting is … certainly not AGI. No, this author’s process is not more rigorous than mine. I’d love to see what his prompt was to make poor Claude produce such drivel. My AI would never.

At no point in the essay is the issue of open-weight models discussed. Perhaps an open-weight model could have drafted his report for him. At no point is any fair, let alone charitable, interpretation offered for the opposing side(s) of this debate.

The essay ends with this line:

“The word is cowardice.”

I’m the kind of person that automatically tries to correct an error when I see it. Yes, I am great at parties. I have a BS-detection reflex and no patience for unearned epistemic authority. Also, nominative determinism compels me to knock people off high horses.

That essay is a series of errors created by a small-minded individual lazily employing AI to produce a poorly informed, slovenly argued stance, after having a small, legitimate gripe. No attempt is made to consider alternative equilibria and their trade-offs. The wild extrapolation from the grave injustice done by Claude’s refusal to a sweeping theory of conniving doomers and hawks is breathtaking. The lack of basic awareness, inability to model the actual arguments of the other side, and unearned sense of moral superiority are awesome to behold.

I think that’s a more appropriate application of “cowardice.”

  1. ^

    “What about ransomware?” Think for 30 seconds about why that’s not really encryption as an attack, per se.

  2. ^

    Uh oh. Seems offense dominant to me.

  3. ^

    Just ask Iran…

item.title: Telephoto Camera: Pixel 10 Pro vs 11 Pro
item.description:
I'm not sophisticated enough to have noticed improvements in the main phone camera in the past 5-10 years, but distance shots are still not very good. The next generation Pixel Pro was supposed to have an improved "telephoto" camera, and when Google Fi offered me a sufficiently good deal [1] I decided to upgrade.

Going from the 10 Pro to the 11 Pro the telephoto camera goes from a 1/2.51" sensor to 1/1.95", and since this is a diagonal measurement this means bringing in ~65% more light. But does it actually take better pictures?

I wandered around taking pairs of pictures, all at 10x. Of this, 5x is optical zoom and the remaining 2x is cropping: I'm showing the pictures as Google Photos gives them to me. All hand-held: while a tripod would likely improve high-zoom pictures, I'm interested in real-world performance which is all going to be hand-held. Every set is the 10 followed by the 11 (taken back-to-back), cropped to 1100x1100.

I started with some well lit things; here's our garden, ~35ft away:

Some construction near our house, ~45ft away:

A neighbor's roof, ~90ft away:

Now some things that are less well-lit. These are in our bedroom with the window open for natural light but only indirect.

A picture Sarah Hirsch painted, ~10ft away:

Our curtains:

Moving to a room with even less light, a poster on the spare room wall, also ~10ft away:

There's some kind of algorithmic cleanup going on, which is especially visible in the words. Is the extra detail in the pictures from the new phone due to it doing a better job of capturing the scene, or is it just making details that look nice? Let's give it an eye exam!

I made a little sheet of random handwritten letters. I could have printed a chart but I hate printers and printers hate me I expect AI-based image processing would overperform on printed text, especially in standard fonts, due to being heavily trained on it. I attached the sheet to the wall:

Just like my own eyes, as the phone gets farther from the sheet it will have more trouble distinguishing the letters, and this will let us see the extent to which it looks better via real details vs made up ones. To get a sense of how hard this is, the top to the bottom of the top "g" is 7/8". Testing with eyes, at 22ft you can just barely make out some of the top-line letters but Lily and I both had mistakes, while at 11ft we could reliably read the top line letters but Lily had several mistakes on the next line.

For this comparison I added Julia's phone, a Pixel 10a, because she didn't object. It would have been better to go back re-do the first part of this post, but I'm too lazy; please pass along a plausible excuse to the peer reviewers. Here's 7ft:

The 10a is already struggling, which makes sense because it doesn't have any optical zoom: it's just cropping to zoom in. Looking at the letters in the bottom row, I think it's running the same image processing and just has less to work with? The letters are already getting a little unnatural in how they're depicted.

The same three at 11ft:

The 10a shows the "t" at the beginning of the second line as a "c", and the third and fourth lines are illegible. The 10 Pro has the third letter of the final line, "a", as "o". The 11 Pro looks noticably better than the 10 Pro, and doesn't seem to have made anything up.

At 22ft:

This is not what the 10a is good at, and we're no longer getting anything useful from it. For the other two this is a real test, just at their level of ability. The top two lines are right for both, but the 11 Pro is clearer. On the 10 Pro, the third line is semi-legible scribbles, and there are some misleading ones: in the third row the last four letters come out as an AI-hallucinated "i g n 5" instead of "s g a s". On the 11 Pro the third line is correct, and it's only the fourth line where it starts swapping letters. Even then, it gets 11/15 correct [2].

It looks to me like the automated cleanup is a common factor across the three Pixels, and the 11 Pro is giving the algorithms more to work with. But I also wouldn't trust any of these phones in cases where correctly capturing details at the limit of the camera's resolution was important.

Overall, this seems like a nice improvement, and worth the hassle of needing to sell my old phone!


[1] Google Fi was offering enough of a discount on a Pixel 11 Pro to bring the cost down below what I think I can sell my 10 Pro for. Specifically, they listed it at $1,100 with a $650 discount, bringing it down to $450 ($477 including tax), and I think my 10 Pro will sell for ~$500. The 11 Pro does have less memory than the 10 Pro (12 GB vs 16 GB, due to the AI-induced shortage) but it still seemed likely worth upgrading for the improved camera and other smaller benefits of running a newer phone. The memory decrease isn't ideal, but looking at how I use my phone I'm not expecting to notice.

[2] I read "t p o t f h p b f a g - r q p" instead of "t y a t f h p b f c g m r q p" which is four mistakes out of fifteen letters.
